text.p: The dollar ended European trading supported but locked in tight ranges as the market counted down to the key U.S. non-farm payrolls data due on Friday.

The U.S. currency again surrendered the limelight to the mark crosses, watching from the wings as money flooded into high yielders and catapulted the Italian lira to a new two-year high and sterling/mark to its best level in 20 months.

"It's all been going on elsewhere today...we've got the non-farm payrolls tomorrow and the market really wanted to wait for them for a clue to which way it was going to move," said Alan Collins, head of technical analysis at Merita Bank.
The dollar was quoted at 1.5300/05 marks and 111.47/54 yen by 1518 GMT, little changed from Wednesday's late European levels of 1.5309/16 and 111.60/65 respectively.

A large sell order in mark/yen pulled dollar/yen towards the lower end of the session's range in late trade, dealers noted, saying that was symptomatic of the dollar's current reliance on external influences for direction.
The mark ended at 72.85/88 yen versus yesterday's 73.17/19.
The U.S. unit continued to receive verbal support, with Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer saying the U.S. had the economic potential and credibility to maintain a strong dollar.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated that a strong dollar was in the interest of the United States. He also said inflation remained low and showed no signs of reigniting.
His comments came as new data showed U.S. August factory orders falling by 1.9 percent, the biggest drop since January 1993, compared to July's 1.7 percent rise.
Weekly U.S. jobless claims numbers released today came in at an unchanged 340,000, although the four-week average rose to 334,500 from 328,750 in the previous week.
Those data failed to move a market which had its attention fixed firmly on tomorrow's payrolls.

Economists polled by Reuters expect September payrolls to have risen on average by 166,000 compared to August's 250,000 increase. The unemployment rate for the same month is seen edging up to 5.2 percent from 5.1.
"There is still a big question mark over which way the dollar will travel if the figures are outside expectations," said a trader at a Swiss bank in London.
The lira was the big winner of the day, romping up to a fresh two-year high of 989.80 per mark amid speculation over an imminent announcement about its re-entry into Europe's exchange rate mechanism.
Sterling glanced 2.4018 marks, its strongest level since February 1995. Both the Italian and UK currencies slipped off highs to stand at 992.05/30 and 2.3940/50 respectively in late Europe.
Elsewhere, the Bank of Spain cut its key money rate to 6.75 percent from 7.25, as expected, and the Bank of Portugal followed its lead with a 15 basis-point trim in its repo rate to 7.10 percent.
